questions.stem: The organ which is sensitive to light in Euglena is the
questions.explanation: The eye spot (stigma), with the photoreceptor at the flagellum base, detects light so Euglena can swim towards it.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a similarity between a typical animal cell and a typical plant cell? Presence of
questions.explanation: Both plant and animal cells have a cell membrane; cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole are plant features.

questions.stem: The first scientist to describe the cell was
questions.explanation: Robert Hooke described and named cells in cork in 1665.

questions.stem: In which of the following parts of a cell is the chromosome found?
questions.explanation: Chromosomes are located in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells.

questions.stem: Which of the following diseases is caused by deficiency of insulin in the body?
questions.explanation: Lack of insulin prevents conversion of glucose to glycogen, causing high blood sugar (diabetes mellitus).

questions.stem: Which of the following is the medium of transportation of nutrients within unicellular organisms?
questions.explanation: Unicellular organisms have no blood system; materials move by diffusion and cytoplasmic streaming in the protoplasm.

questions.stem: Which of the following blood vessels carries oxygenated blood into the heart?
questions.explanation: The pulmonary vein returns oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

questions.stem: The conditions that ensure successful exchange of gases in multicellular organisms include the following except
options: concentration gradient across the respiratory surface.
presence of thin membrane as the respiratory surface.
presence of large surface area of the respiratory organ.
presence of small, dry surface area of the respiratory organ.
questions.explanation: Respiratory surfaces must be large and moist; a small, dry surface would hinder gas exchange.

questions.stem: The respiratory organ found in the cockroach is the
questions.explanation: Insects breathe through a tracheal system opening at spiracles.

questions.stem: Which of the following structures functions as an excretory system found in flat worms?
questions.explanation: Flatworms (e.g. planaria, tapeworm) excrete by flame cells; nephridia are in annelids and Malpighian tubules in insects.

questions.stem: Which of the following organs is associated with deamination of proteins?
questions.explanation: Excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver, forming urea.

questions.stem: Ultrafiltration in the kidney takes place in the
questions.explanation: High pressure in the glomerulus forces filtrate into Bowman's capsule (ultrafiltration).

questions.stem: When an axon is at rest, the concentration of ions on either side of the membrane are different. Which of the following is correct about the concentrations of ions on either side of the membrane?
options: There is an excess of potassium ions inside the axon and an excess of sodium ions outside.
The inside of the axon becomes positively charged while the outside is negatively charged.
There is an excess of sodium ions on the inner side of the axon.
Chloride and potassium ions begin to move across the membrane.
Calcium ions accumulate on the inner side of the axon.
questions.explanation: At resting potential the sodium-potassium pump keeps K+ high inside and Na+ high outside; the inside is negative.

questions.stem: The groups of sensory cells found on the upper surface of the tongue are called
questions.explanation: Taste receptors are grouped in taste buds on the tongue.

questions.stem: Which of the following mineral salts is a trace element?
questions.explanation: Zinc is needed in minute amounts (trace/micro-element); the others are macro-elements.

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms reduces nitrates in the soil to gaseous nitrogen?
questions.explanation: Denitrifying bacteria (e.g. Pseudomonas) convert nitrates to free nitrogen.

questions.stem: The process whereby microorganisms can convert atmospheric nitrogen into nitrogenous compound is known as
questions.explanation: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria such as Rhizobium and Azotobacter fix atmospheric nitrogen into compounds.

questions.stem: What type of relationship exists between a tapeworm and an infected mammal?
questions.explanation: The tapeworm benefits by feeding on digested food while harming the host: parasitism.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a marine habitat? A large body of water
options: which has no distinctive colour or taste
questions.explanation: Marine habitats (seas and oceans) are characterised by high salinity.

questions.stem: The following are features of the tropical rain forest except
options: short trees growing beneath tall trees.
questions.explanation: Rain forest has dense, tall, broad-leaved trees in layers; scanty small-leaved trees describe arid vegetation.

questions.stem: The following are features of Northern Guinea Savanna except
options: presence of tall trees with thick bark.
bare soil with very few trees.
questions.explanation: Northern Guinea savanna has tall grasses and fire-resistant woody trees; bare soil with few trees is typical of drier Sahel areas.

questions.stem: Which of the following explains the term pyramid of numbers?
options: The number of organisms in a trophic level
The relationship between plants in different trophic levels
The number of saprophytes and parasites in a habitat
The number of predators in a habitat
Progressive decrease in the number of individuals from lower to higher trophic level
questions.explanation: A pyramid of numbers shows numbers decreasing from producers up to top consumers.

questions.stem: In which of the following processes is carbon dioxide not given out?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and releases oxygen.

questions.stem: Sea water taken in by a living organism can be recycled into the atmosphere through all the following processes except
questions.explanation: Water returns to the air through transpiration, excretion, respiration and decay; digestion uses water in hydrolysis and returns none to the air.

questions.stem: Which of the following water pollutants may contain organisms that cause dysentery?
questions.explanation: Untreated sewage carries faecal pathogens such as Entamoeba and Shigella that cause dysentery.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an adaptation of plants or animals to desert environment?
options: Metabolic waste in the form of uric acid in some animals
questions.explanation: Broad leaves lose much water by transpiration; desert plants have reduced leaves or spines.

questions.stem: A climax community is characterised by
options: a stable composition of plant and animal species.
rapid changes in the composition of species.
constant changes in appearance of the habitat.
different species occurring at different times.
questions.explanation: A climax community is the stable, self-perpetuating final stage of succession.

questions.stem: The use of predators or parasites to control pests in the farm is known as
questions.explanation: Using natural enemies to reduce pest populations is biological control.

questions.stem: Which of the following substances cannot control the growth of harmful microorganisms?
questions.explanation: An isotonic sugar solution causes no water loss from microbes and can even feed them; hypertonic salt dehydrates them.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the underlining principle in the adoption of biological control of pests?
options: Knowledge of agricultural practices by the farmer
The presence of poisonous chemicals in the farm
The relative population of plants and animals in the farm
The predator-prey relationship in the ecological community
questions.explanation: Biological control depends on natural enemies (predators/parasites) keeping pest numbers down.

questions.stem: The following agencies are responsible for conservation in Nigeria except
options: Ministry of Agriculture and Natural Resources.
questions.explanation: The Red Cross is a humanitarian organisation, not a conservation agency.

questions.stem:
The table below indicates the result of an experiment during which grains of different colours in two maize cobs were counted.
Maize cob I: White 30, Pink 60, Red 30.
Maize cob II: White 50, Pink 99, Red 49.
Which of the following ratios agrees with the result?
questions.explanation: 30:60:30 = 1:2:1 and 50:99:49 is about 1:2:1, the ratio for incomplete dominance in an F2.

questions.stem: One of the factors that must be considered for safe blood transfusion is
options: rhesus factors of the donor and the recipient.
questions.explanation: Blood group (ABO) and rhesus factor compatibility must be checked to avoid agglutination.

questions.stem: One of the major criticisms against Mendelian laws is that they do not recognise that
options: one trait is often controlled by many pairs of genes.
single factor inheritance is never a reality.
questions.explanation: Mendel assumed one gene pair per trait; many traits are polygenic.

questions.stem: Identical twins inherit their genes from
options: the same ovum and different sperms.
the same sperm and different ova.
the same ovum and the same sperm.
questions.explanation: Identical twins arise from one zygote (one ovum fertilised by one sperm) that splits into two.

questions.stem: The offspring produced when pure strains interbreed is described as
questions.explanation: Crossing two different pure (homozygous) strains produces hybrids.

questions.stem: Which of the following diseases or disorders can be prevented by the application of the knowledge of heredity through marriage counselling?
questions.explanation: Couples who know their haemoglobin genotypes (e.g. AS x AS) can avoid producing SS children through genetic counselling.

questions.stem:
Study the genetic cross below showing the inheritance of blood groups: the father has alleles A and B (blood group AB) and the mother has alleles A and O; each parent's gametes combine to give four F1 offspring.
From the cross above, which of the following F1 offspring does not belong to the father?
questions.explanation: The father (AB) must pass on A or B, so every child gets A or B from him; OO cannot be his child. The F1 are AA, AO, AB and BO.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a function of the chromosome?
questions.explanation: Chromosomes carry the genes that transmit hereditary traits.

questions.stem: Which of the following does not illustrate adaptation to the environment?
options: Development of big muscles by a weight lifter
questions.explanation: Muscles built by training are acquired and not inherited, so they are not an adaptation.

questions.stem: The changing of colour by a chameleon to that of the environment is an example of
questions.explanation: Matching the background (camouflage) protects the chameleon from predators and helps it ambush prey.

questions.stem: The division of labour in social insects is an example of
questions.explanation: Castes in termites and bees performing different tasks is a behavioural adaptation of social insects.

questions.stem: The swarming especially at the beginning of the rainy season is a courtship behaviour shown by
questions.explanation: Winged reproductive termites (alates) swarm in the early rains to pair and found new colonies.

questions.stem: Lamarck's evolution theory could be summarised by the statement that
options: only the fittest can survive in a challenging environment.
species that are unable to adapt become extinct.
new characteristics do not arise in organisms in time of need.
the changing environment imposes structural, physiological and behavioural changes in organisms.
in a changing and unstable environment nature rejects the weak.
questions.explanation: Lamarck held that environmental needs cause changes (use and disuse) that are then inherited.

questions.topic: Ecological Components: Lithosphere, Hydrosphere, Atmosphere and Niche
questions.stem: The property of clay soil that prevents it from supporting thick vegetation is its
options: possession of chemically weathered granite rocks.
porosity and low water retention ability.
high capillary spaces between the soil particles.
questions.explanation: Clay has tiny pores and poor drainage, so it becomes waterlogged and poorly aerated.

questions.stem:
(a)(i) List two diseases each of plants and animals caused by bacteria.
(ii) State three ways in which bacteria are useful.
(b) State three methods by which mosquitoes can be controlled and state the reason for each method.
(c) Describe an experiment to demonstrate the presence of bacteria under the finger nails.
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Plant diseases: e.g. bacterial blight of cassava, soft rot, wilt of tomato, citrus canker (any two)
2 marks: (a)(i) Animal diseases: e.g. tuberculosis, cholera, typhoid, gonorrhoea, anthrax, tetanus (any two)
3 marks: (a)(ii) Nitrogen fixation; decay/recycling of nutrients; making yoghurt/cheese or retting; producing antibiotics; digestion of cellulose in ruminants (any three)
2 marks: (b) Draining stagnant water/clearing bushes - removes breeding sites
2 marks: (b) Spraying oil/larvicide on water - suffocates or kills larvae and pupae
2 marks: (b) Spraying insecticides/using nets and screens or introducing larva-eating fish (Tilapia/Gambusia) - kills adults or prevents bites / eats larvae
2 marks: (c) Sterilise two nutrient agar plates; scrape under the finger nail with a sterile wire/press nail on agar in one plate; leave the other untouched as control; cover both
2 marks: (c) Incubate at about 37 degrees C (or room temperature) for 2-3 days
3 marks: (c) Colonies appear on the inoculated plate but not on the control, showing bacteria were present under the finger nail
questions.explanation: (a)(i) Bacterial plant diseases include bacterial blight of cassava and soft rot of vegetables; bacterial animal diseases include tuberculosis and cholera. (ii) Bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen, decompose dead matter to recycle nutrients, and are used in industry, e.g. making yoghurt and cheese and producing antibiotics. (b) Draining or filling stagnant pools and clearing bushes removes breeding grounds; spraying oil or larvicide on water surfaces kills larvae and pupae by suffocation or poisoning; spraying insecticides or using treated nets and window screens kills adults or prevents bites; stocking ponds with larva-eating fish gives biological control. (c) Sterilise two Petri dishes of nutrient agar. Scrape under a finger nail with a sterilised wire loop and streak it on one plate (or press the nail on it); leave the other as a control. Cover, seal and incubate warm for 2-3 days. Colonies appear on the experimental plate but not on the control, proving that bacteria were present under the nail.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe the process of inhalation in man.
(b) Describe briefly the process of gaseous exchange in the shoot system of flowering plants.
(c) Describe an experiment to demonstrate the effect of distilled water on mammalian red blood cell.
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) The external intercostal muscles contract and internal ones relax, raising the ribs upwards and outwards
2 marks: (a) The diaphragm muscles contract and the diaphragm flattens/moves downwards
2 marks: (a) The volume of the thoracic cavity increases and pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure
2 marks: (a) Air rushes in through the nostrils, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles into the alveoli, which inflate
2 marks: (b) Gases enter and leave through stomata on leaves (and lenticels on woody stems)
2 marks: (b) Gases diffuse through intercellular air spaces and dissolve in the moist cell surfaces of mesophyll cells
2 marks: (b) In light, CO2 diffuses in and O2 out (photosynthesis exceeds respiration); in darkness O2 diffuses in and CO2 out
2 marks: (c) Place a drop of fresh blood in distilled water on a slide (and a drop in normal saline as control) and observe under the microscope
2 marks: (c) Water enters the red cells by osmosis since distilled water is hypotonic
2 marks: (c) The cells swell and burst (haemolysis), while the control cells keep their shape
questions.explanation: (a) During inhalation the external intercostal muscles contract, pulling the ribs upwards and outwards, while the diaphragm muscles contract so that the dome-shaped diaphragm flattens. Both actions enlarge the thoracic cavity, lowering the pressure inside the lungs below atmospheric pressure, so air flows in through the nose, pharynx, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles into the alveoli. (b) In the shoot, gases pass through stomata (and lenticels in stems) into intercellular air spaces and dissolve in the moist walls of mesophyll cells. In daylight, carbon dioxide diffuses in for photosynthesis and oxygen diffuses out; at night respiration dominates, so oxygen enters and carbon dioxide leaves. (c) Put a drop of fresh mammalian blood into distilled water and another into 0.9% saline (control). After a few minutes view both under a microscope. Cells in distilled water swell and burst (haemolysis) because water enters them by osmosis from the hypotonic medium; cells in saline remain normal.

questions.stem:
(a) Give a brief description of the characteristics of the Northern Guinea savanna.
(b) Describe how you can estimate the density of a plant species using a quadrat.
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Moderate rainfall (about 1000-1500 mm) with a distinct long dry season of about 5-6 months
2 marks: (a) High temperatures and low humidity in the dry season; harmattan influence
2 marks: (a) Vegetation of tall grasses (e.g. elephant grass, Andropogon) with scattered trees
2 marks: (a) Trees are fire-resistant with thick bark, deep roots and are often deciduous (e.g. shea butter, locust bean, Isoberlinia)
2 marks: (a) Bush fires are common in the dry season; animals include many herbivores (antelopes, grasscutters) and predators
3 marks: (b) Throw a quadrat (e.g. 1 m x 1 m frame) at random several times in the area
3 marks: (b) Count the number of individuals of the plant species in each quadrat and record
2 marks: (b) Find the average number per quadrat
2 marks: (b) Density = average number of individuals per quadrat / area of the quadrat (e.g. per square metre)
questions.explanation: (a) The Northern Guinea savanna has a fairly long dry season of five to six months and annual rainfall of roughly 1000-1500 mm, with high temperatures and dry harmattan winds. The vegetation is tall grassland, e.g. Andropogon and elephant grass, interspersed with scattered trees such as Isoberlinia, shea butter and locust bean. The trees have thick, fire-resistant bark, deep roots and often shed their leaves in the dry season, because bush fires are frequent. Many herbivores such as antelopes and grasscutters occur, together with their predators. (b) Make a quadrat, e.g. a 1 m square frame. Throw it at random about ten times in the area. Count and record the number of individuals of the chosen species inside it each time. Calculate the mean number per throw, then divide by the area of the quadrat to obtain density, e.g. plants per square metre; this can be multiplied by the total area to estimate population.

questions.stem:
(a) List four characters which can be transmitted from parent to offspring in man.
(b) State two differences between mitosis and meiosis.
(c) Explain briefly the importance of meiosis and fertilization in the reproduction of organisms.
(d) In a monohybrid cross between a pure breeding plant that produces blue flowers and a pure breeding plant that produces white flowers, the F1 generation produced only blue flowers. By means of labelled cross diagrams, state the type of flowers you would expect if the F1 generation is
(i) self-pollinated;
(ii) cross-pollinated with a pure breeding plant that produces white flowers.
Give reasons for your answers in (d)(i) and (ii).
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Any four: skin colour, height, blood group, eye colour, hair type/colour, tongue rolling, sickle cell trait, colour blindness, haemophilia, shape of ear lobe
2 marks: (b) Mitosis gives two daughter cells while meiosis gives four
2 marks: (b) Mitosis keeps the chromosome number (diploid) while meiosis halves it (haploid); crossing over occurs only in meiosis
2 marks: (c) Meiosis halves the chromosome number in gametes, so the diploid number is restored at fertilisation and kept constant from generation to generation
2 marks: (c) Meiosis (crossing over, independent assortment) and fertilisation (random fusion of gametes) produce variation
1 mark: (d) Let B = blue (dominant), b = white; F1 is Bb
3 marks: (d)(i) Bb x Bb gives gametes B, b and B, b; offspring BB, Bb, Bb, bb
2 marks: (d)(i) 3 blue : 1 white, because blue is dominant and white shows only when homozygous recessive
2 marks: (d)(ii) Bb x bb gives gametes B, b and b; offspring Bb, Bb, bb, bb
2 marks: (d)(ii) 1 blue : 1 white (50% each), because half the offspring receive the dominant B allele
questions.explanation: (a) Inherited human characters include skin colour, eye colour, blood group, height and tongue rolling (also sickle cell trait, haemophilia). (b) Mitosis produces two daughter cells, meiosis four; mitosis keeps the diploid chromosome number, while meiosis halves it and involves crossing over and pairing of homologous chromosomes. (c) Meiosis forms haploid gametes so that fertilisation restores the diploid number, keeping chromosome number constant across generations; crossing over, independent assortment and random fusion of gametes produce genetic variation for evolution and adaptation. (d) Blue (B) is dominant to white (b); parents BB x bb give F1 Bb, all blue. (i) Self-pollination Bb x Bb gives gametes B and b from each parent; offspring BB : Bb : bb = 1 : 2 : 1, i.e. 3 blue : 1 white, because only bb plants lack the dominant allele. (ii) Backcross Bb x bb gives Bb and bb in equal numbers: 1 blue : 1 white, because the white parent can only supply b and half the F1 gametes carry B.

questions.stem: All animals are dependent on green plants because, plants
options: shelter them from excessive heat from the sun.
are used for building houses and furniture.
questions.explanation: Green plants are the producers; all animals depend directly or indirectly on the food they make by photosynthesis.

questions.stem: The scientist who discovered the cell while examining a thin slice of cork under the microscope was
questions.explanation: Robert Hooke observed and named cells in cork in 1665.

questions.topic: Uptake and movement of water and mineral salts in plants
questions.stem: The two important physical processes involved in the absorption and transport of materials in plants are
questions.explanation: Water enters root hairs by osmosis and mineral ions and gases move by diffusion.

questions.stem: The process by which plants manufacture food from carbon dioxide and water, using energy from the sun is termed
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis uses light energy trapped by chlorophyll to make sugar from CO2 and water.

questions.stem: The process in which insects undergo conspicuous changes in form and appearance during development is known as
questions.explanation: Metamorphosis is the series of changes in form, e.g. egg-larva-pupa-adult.

questions.stem: Diagrams I, II and III illustrate the feet of birds adapted to various modes of feeding and movement. The foot labelled III is strong and has blunt claws on its digits. This implies that the bird
options: uses the foot to scratch the soil.
uses the foot to supplement wing action in flight.
questions.explanation: Strong feet with blunt claws, as in the domestic fowl, are used to scratch the soil for food.

questions.stem: Diagrams I, II and III illustrate the feet of birds adapted to various modes of feeding and movement. The long and sharp claws in the foot labelled II show that the bird uses them to
questions.explanation: Long, sharp curved claws (talons), as in the hawk, grip and hold prey.

questions.stem: Conventional method of sewage disposal involves all the following except defaecating
questions.explanation: Defaecating in open fields is an unsanitary practice, not a method of sewage disposal.

questions.stem: Which of the following actions is not an example of a simple reflex action?
options: Withdrawal of hand from hot object
questions.explanation: Reading is a learned, voluntary activity involving the brain; the others are automatic reflexes.

questions.topic: Forms in which Living Cells Exist
questions.stem: In which of the following is a cellulose cell wall present?
questions.explanation: Spirogyra is a green alga (plant-like) with a cellulose wall; the others are animal cells.

questions.topic: Forms in which Living Cells Exist
questions.stem: Which of the following organisms exists as a filament?
questions.explanation: Spirogyra consists of cells joined end to end in filaments; Volvox is colonial and the others are single cells.

questions.stem: All the following can illustrate the dynamic nature of the ecosystem except
questions.explanation: Cycling of nitrogen, carbon, water and nutrients shows the ecosystem's dynamic exchange; locomotion does not.

questions.stem: Which of the following measures does not ensure conservation?
options: Enclosing fishes in ponds where they will not be stolen
questions.explanation: Keeping fish in ponds to stop theft is a security measure, not conservation of natural resources.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not required for primary production to occur in plants?
questions.explanation: Sugar is the product of photosynthesis, not a requirement.

questions.stem: Which of the following blood group(s) is/are the universal donor(s)?
questions.explanation: Group O red cells carry no A or B antigens, so O can be given to all groups.

questions.stem: The branch of science which deals with resemblances, origin and expression of biological variations is called
questions.explanation: Genetics is the study of heredity and variation.

questions.stem: Which of the following can cause desert encroachment?
questions.explanation: Overgrazing removes plant cover, exposing soil to erosion and desertification.

questions.stem: The morphological, physiological and behavioural characteristics which enable an organism to survive in its environment is called
questions.explanation: Features that fit an organism to survive in its environment are adaptations.

questions.stem: Which of the following performs the same function as the contractile vacuole of a unicellular organism?
questions.explanation: The contractile vacuole carries out osmoregulation and excretion, which the kidney performs in mammals.

questions.stem: Which of the following represents the correct order in a possible food chain?
questions.explanation: Diatoms are producers eaten by small crustaceans, which are eaten by fish, which are eaten by man.

questions.stem: Which of the following relationships illustrates competition?
options: Cattle egret moving along with cattle
Goats and cows grazing on a small grass lawn
Mosses succeeding lichens in a rocky terrain
Red mangrove swamp dying and replaced by white mangrove
Forest trees, shrubs and grasses replacing white mangrove in a swamp
questions.explanation: Goats and cows compete for the same limited grass; the others are commensalism or succession.

questions.stem: The structure used by fishes to detect the presence and movement of other animals by the vibration they produce is the
questions.explanation: The lateral line system detects pressure waves and vibrations in water.

questions.topic: Skeleton and supporting systems in animals
questions.stem: Muscles are attached to bones by means of
questions.explanation: Tendons join muscle to bone; ligaments join bone to bone.

questions.stem: The ability of the eye to alter the focal length of the lens, with regard to the distance of the object from the eye is known as
questions.explanation: Accommodation is the change in lens curvature by ciliary muscles to focus near or distant objects.

questions.topic: Development of the zygote in flowering plants
questions.stem: What is the fate of the ovary of a flower after fertilization? It
questions.explanation: After fertilisation the ovary develops into the fruit and the ovules into seeds.

questions.topic: Linkage, sex determination and sex-linked characters
questions.stem:
The table below is a Punnett square for sex determination in man: the eggs each carry X; the sperms carry either X or Y; the offspring are XX, XX, XY and XY.
Which of the following determines a normal male offspring?
questions.explanation: A male has one X and one Y chromosome (XY).

questions.stem:
The table below is a Punnett square for sex determination in man: the eggs each carry X; the sperms carry either X or Y; the offspring are XX, XX, XY and XY.
What is the theoretical probability that a normal male child will be born?
questions.explanation: Two of the four combinations are XY, so the probability is 2/4 = 1/2.

questions.topic: Skeleton and supporting systems in animals
questions.stem: Which of these is not part of the appendicular skeleton?
questions.explanation: The vertebral column belongs to the axial skeleton; girdles and limb bones are appendicular.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors does not control population growth?
questions.explanation: Abundant food encourages population growth; the others limit it.

questions.stem: The following conditions form the basis of competition in a habitat except
questions.explanation: Organisms compete for limited resources such as food, space, mates and light, not for body structure.

questions.stem: The part of the ear which equalises air pressure on either side of the eardrum is the
questions.explanation: The Eustachian tube links the middle ear to the pharynx and equalises pressure.

questions.stem: Mutation leads to evolution in that it
options: gives rise to offspring which have the same characteristics as the parents.
kills all organisms where it has occurred.
gives rise to new individuals which differ considerably from their parents.
always confers adaptability to the offspring.
does not confer adaptability to the offspring.
questions.explanation: Mutations produce new heritable variations on which natural selection acts.

questions.stem: The process whereby poisonous compounds are made harmless in the liver is called
questions.explanation: The liver detoxifies poisons such as alcohol and drugs.

questions.stem: The deficiency of calcium in a plant may result in
options: stunted growth and poor root development.
poor growth, leaves become orange or brown.
stunted growth, slender stem and yellowing of leaves.
very small leaves and yellowing of leaves.
questions.explanation: Calcium is needed for cell wall formation and growing points; its lack causes stunted growth and poor root development.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the least safe method of birth control? Using
questions.explanation: Withdrawal often fails because sperm may be released before ejaculation.

questions.stem: The gradual, cumulative, adaptive and heritable changes in an organism over a long period of time resulting in emergence of new species is known as
questions.explanation: Organic evolution is the gradual change of organisms over long periods giving rise to new species.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a pollution control measure?
options: Penalising those who dump refuse on water or land
Controlling the emission of smoke from automobiles and industries
Ensuring that there is no spillage of oil
Establishing government agencies like Federal Environmental Protection Agency (FEPA)
questions.explanation: Discharging sewage into streams pollutes water.

questions.stem: Which pair of structures contributes to balance in mammals?
questions.explanation: The utriculus and sacculus (with the semicircular canals) detect posture and balance.

questions.stem: Spermatogenesis and Oogenesis are both terms used to describe
questions.explanation: Spermatogenesis and oogenesis are the formation of male and female gametes, i.e. gametogenesis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a continuous variation?
questions.explanation: Tongue rolling is either present or absent (discontinuous); the others show a range of values.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a conservable natural resource?
questions.explanation: Sunlight is inexhaustible and cannot be conserved or stored by man in nature.

questions.stem: Which of the following plant diseases is indicated when grains of cereals are covered with a mass of spores?
questions.explanation: In smut the grains are replaced by black masses of fungal spores.

questions.stem: Which of the following structural features in animals does not affect control of body temperature?
questions.explanation: Fur, feathers, skin and its capillaries regulate heat loss; scales in fish and reptiles do not regulate temperature.

questions.stem: The control of water and salt requirements of the body in order to maintain a stable internal environment is known as
questions.explanation: Maintaining a constant internal environment, including water and salt balance, is homeostasis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a condition necessary for germination to occur in most seeds?
questions.explanation: Seeds need water, oxygen and suitable temperature; they germinate on moist cotton wool without soil.

questions.topic: Modes of Nutrition (autotrophic, chemosynthetic and carnivorous plants)
questions.stem: Which of the following structural features adapts Drosera (Sundew) to its carnivorous mode of nutrition?
questions.explanation: Sundew leaves have sticky club-shaped glandular tentacles that trap and digest insects.

questions.stem: Which of the following terms is not associated with finger prints?
questions.explanation: Fingerprint patterns are arch, loop, whorl and compound; a suture is a skull joint.

questions.stem: In human beings the albino trait is recessive and the normal skin colour is dominant. Therefore the probability of parents that are heterozygous for albinism, having an albino child is
questions.explanation: Aa x Aa gives AA, Aa, Aa, aa; only aa (1 in 4) is albino.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the carrier of hereditary material?
questions.explanation: Chromosomes carry the genes (DNA).

questions.stem: Which of these statements is correct in the human ABO blood grouping system?
options: O has antigens A and B
A and B are both recessive
questions.explanation: A and B are codominant and both dominant to O, which is recessive.

questions.stem: In man, adult Schistosoma is found in the
questions.explanation: Adult Schistosoma haematobium lives in the veins around the urinary bladder.

questions.topic: Skeleton and supporting systems in animals
questions.stem: Which of the following structures does not function as support in animals?
questions.explanation: The cuticle (exoskeleton), cartilage, bone and the earthworm's hydrostatic skeleton all give support; scales on birds' legs only protect.

questions.stem:
(a) List three major zones in the marine habitat stating one characteristic feature of each zone.
(b)(i) Give one example each of plants and animals in the marine habitat.
(ii) Explain how each of the plant and animal is adapted to the habitat.
(c) State three behavioural adaptations of animals to seasonal changes in terrestrial habitat.
(d) State three characteristics each of the plant community in the tropical rain forest and savanna.
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Intertidal/littoral zone: alternately covered and exposed by tides; organisms face desiccation and wave action
2 marks: (a) Neritic zone: shallow water over the continental shelf, well lit and rich in plankton/nutrients
1 mark: (a) Oceanic/pelagic (including abyssal) zone: deep open sea; light absent at depth, high pressure, low temperature
1 mark: (b)(i) Plant: e.g. Sargassum/seaweed (brown alga) or phytoplankton (diatoms)
1 mark: (b)(i) Animal: e.g. crab, periwinkle, barnacle, fish, oyster
2 marks: (b)(ii) Plant: holdfast for attachment against waves, mucilage to prevent drying, air bladders for floating near light
2 marks: (b)(ii) Animal: e.g. crab has hard exoskeleton against waves and desiccation, gills for breathing, claws; or barnacle has shell closing at low tide and cement for attachment
1 mark: (c) Migration to areas with more food/water (e.g. birds)
1 mark: (c) Hibernation in cold or aestivation in dry season (e.g. snails, lungfish)
1 mark: (c) Food storage/burrowing or changing feeding/breeding time with seasons (e.g. squirrels, termites swarming in the rains)
3 marks: (d) Rain forest: tall trees in layers/stratification with a closed canopy; evergreen broad leaves; many climbers/epiphytes and buttress roots; little undergrowth
3 marks: (d) Savanna: grasses dominant with scattered trees; trees short, often deciduous with thick fire-resistant bark; deep roots; grasses dry up in the dry season
questions.explanation: (a) The marine habitat has the intertidal (littoral) zone, between high and low tide marks, which is exposed at low tide so organisms face drying and strong wave action; the neritic zone, the shallow, sunlit water over the continental shelf that is rich in plankton and nutrients; and the oceanic (pelagic) zone of open deep sea, whose depths (abyssal zone) are dark, cold and under great pressure. (b) A marine plant is Sargassum (a seaweed); it has a holdfast for anchorage, a mucilaginous coat to resist drying and air bladders that keep it floating in light. A marine animal is the crab; its hard exoskeleton resists waves and drying, it breathes by gills and it burrows or hides in crevices at low tide. (c) Animals respond to seasons by migrating (birds), hibernating or aestivating (lungfish, snails), and storing food or breeding at favourable times (e.g. termites swarming at the start of the rains). (d) Rain forest plants are tall, evergreen, broad-leaved trees in layers with a closed canopy, many climbers and epiphytes, and buttress roots. Savanna plants are mainly grasses with scattered short trees, which are often deciduous, have thick fire-resistant bark and deep roots.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe the general arrangement of the viscera of a named mammal.
(b) Describe the process of feeding in:
(i) Hydra;
(ii) Amoeba.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) Named mammal, e.g. rabbit/rat
2 marks: (a) The body cavity is divided by the diaphragm into the thoracic cavity in front and the abdominal cavity behind
2 marks: (a) Thorax: heart in the pericardium between the two lungs (in pleural cavities); trachea and oesophagus pass through
2 marks: (a) Abdomen: stomach on the left below the diaphragm; liver (lobed, with gall bladder) just below the diaphragm; coiled small intestine held by mesentery; pancreas in the loop of the duodenum; spleen near the stomach
2 marks: (a) Large intestine (caecum, appendix, colon, rectum); kidneys on the dorsal wall with ureters to the bladder; reproductive organs in the posterior abdomen/pelvic region
2 marks: (b)(i) Hydra catches small animals (e.g. Daphnia) with its tentacles; nematoblasts discharge threads that paralyse and hold the prey
2 marks: (b)(i) The tentacles push the prey through the mouth into the enteron (gut cavity)
2 marks: (b)(i) Gland cells secrete enzymes for extracellular digestion; food particles are engulfed by endoderm cells for intracellular digestion; undigested remains pass out through the mouth
2 marks: (b)(ii) Amoeba moves towards food and puts out pseudopodia that surround the food particle (phagocytosis)
2 marks: (b)(ii) The food is enclosed in a food vacuole with a little water
1 mark: (b)(ii) Enzymes are secreted into the vacuole and digest the food; soluble products diffuse into the cytoplasm and are assimilated; undigested matter is egested anywhere on the surface
questions.explanation: (a) In the rabbit the body cavity is divided by the muscular diaphragm into thorax and abdomen. In the thorax the heart, enclosed in the pericardium, lies between the two lungs in their pleural cavities, with the trachea and oesophagus running through. In the abdomen, the large lobed liver with its gall bladder lies just behind the diaphragm; the stomach lies on the left, leading to the duodenum, in whose loop the pancreas lies; the spleen lies beside the stomach; the long coiled ileum is held by mesenteries and leads to the large caecum and appendix, colon and rectum. The kidneys lie against the dorsal wall, their ureters leading to the bladder, and the reproductive organs lie posteriorly. (b)(i) Hydra captures small animals such as water fleas with its tentacles; stinging cells (nematoblasts) discharge threads that paralyse and hold the prey, which the tentacles push through the mouth into the enteron. Gland cells secrete enzymes that partly digest it; small particles are engulfed by endoderm cells and digested intracellularly; undigested remains are ejected through the mouth. (ii) Amoeba flows towards food and surrounds it with pseudopodia, engulfing it in a food vacuole. Enzymes are secreted into the vacuole and digest the food; the soluble products diffuse into the cytoplasm and are assimilated, and undigested remains are egested at any point on the surface as the amoeba moves away.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe an experiment to demonstrate the effect of auxin on growth of a plant shoot.
(b) List three uses of auxin in agriculture.
(c) Describe the mechanism of transmission of impulses through a nerve fibre.
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Use oat/maize coleoptiles (seedlings); cut off the tips of some and place them on agar blocks for some time so that auxin diffuses into the agar
2 marks: (a) Place the auxin-agar block on one side of a decapitated coleoptile; place a plain agar block on another decapitated coleoptile as control; keep in darkness
2 marks: (a) After some hours, the coleoptile with the auxin block on one side bends away from that side; the control does not grow/bend
2 marks: (a) Conclusion: auxin causes growth by cell elongation on the side where it is more concentrated
1 mark: (b) Rooting of stem cuttings
1 mark: (b) Selective weedicides/herbicides (e.g. 2,4-D)
1 mark: (b) Producing parthenocarpic (seedless) fruits, preventing premature fruit drop or inducing flowering/fruit setting
2 marks: (c) At rest the axon membrane is polarised: outside positive with more Na+ ions, inside negative with more K+ ions (resting potential)
2 marks: (c) A stimulus makes the membrane permeable to Na+, which rush in, reversing the charge (depolarisation/action potential)
2 marks: (c) K+ then diffuse out, restoring the resting potential (repolarisation); the sodium-potassium pump restores the ion balance
2 marks: (c) The local current depolarises the next part of the membrane, so the impulse travels as a wave along the fibre; in myelinated fibres it jumps between nodes of Ranvier
1 mark: (c) At the synapse, the impulse releases a transmitter (e.g. acetylcholine) which crosses the gap to the next neurone
questions.explanation: (a) Cut the tips from several oat coleoptiles and stand them on agar blocks for about an hour so that auxin diffuses into the agar. Place such an agar block on one side of the cut stump of another coleoptile, and a plain agar block on a second stump as control; keep both in darkness. After a few hours the coleoptile carrying the auxin block bends away from the side with the block, while the control shows little growth. This shows auxin promotes growth by cell elongation where it is concentrated. (b) In agriculture auxins are used to promote rooting of cuttings, as selective weedkillers (2,4-D), and to produce seedless fruits or prevent premature fruit drop. (c) In a resting nerve fibre the membrane is polarised, positive outside (high Na+) and negative inside (high K+). A stimulus makes the membrane permeable to sodium ions, which rush in and reverse the charge, producing an action potential. Potassium ions then diffuse out to restore the resting potential, and the sodium-potassium pump re-establishes the ion distribution. The local current depolarises the adjacent region, so the impulse is propagated along the fibre as a wave of depolarisation; in myelinated fibres it jumps from node to node. At the synapse a chemical transmitter carries the impulse to the next neurone.

questions.stem:
(a)(i) Explain the term courtship behaviour in animals.
(ii) How does courtship aid reproduction in animals?
(b) Describe the process of fertilization in flowering plants.
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Courtship behaviour is the set of activities (displays, calls, dances, gifts) performed by animals, usually the male, to attract and win a mate of the same species before mating
1 mark: (a)(i) Examples: display of feathers by the peacock/cock, croaking of male toads, swarming of termites, dancing of birds
2 marks: (a)(ii) It helps individuals recognise and attract mates of the same species, preventing cross-species mating
2 marks: (a)(ii) It brings sexes together and synchronises their readiness so that gametes are released at the same time, increasing the chance of fertilisation
2 marks: (a)(ii) It allows selection of the fittest mate and reduces aggression between partners
2 marks: (b) After pollination the pollen grain absorbs sugary fluid on the stigma and germinates, producing a pollen tube
2 marks: (b) The pollen tube grows down the style, digesting its way, controlled by the tube nucleus; the generative nucleus divides to form two male nuclei
2 marks: (b) The tube enters the ovule through the micropyle and bursts in the embryo sac, releasing the two male nuclei
2 marks: (b) One male nucleus fuses with the egg nucleus to form the diploid zygote
2 marks: (b) The other fuses with the two polar nuclei (or definitive nucleus) to form the triploid endosperm nucleus; this is double fertilisation
1 mark: (b) The zygote develops into the embryo, the ovule into the seed and the ovary into the fruit
questions.explanation: (a)(i) Courtship behaviour is the series of special displays, sounds or actions by which an animal, usually the male, attracts and wins a mate of its own species before mating, e.g. the peacock spreading its tail, male toads croaking, cocks dancing round hens, and the swarming of winged termites. (ii) Courtship ensures that mates of the same species recognise each other, brings the sexes together and prepares them physiologically so that mating and release of gametes are synchronised, increases the chance of fertilisation, allows the selection of strong mates and reduces aggression. (b) After pollination the pollen grain absorbs sugary fluid on the stigma and germinates, putting out a pollen tube that grows down the style under the control of the tube nucleus, while the generative nucleus divides into two male nuclei. The tube enters the ovule through the micropyle and releases the two male nuclei into the embryo sac. One fuses with the egg cell to form the diploid zygote; the other fuses with the polar (definitive) nucleus to form the triploid primary endosperm nucleus. This double fertilisation is followed by development of the zygote into the embryo, the ovule into a seed and the ovary into a fruit.

questions.stem: Which of the following structures is found in animal cells?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes occur in all cells; cell walls, middle lamella and pyrenoids are plant/algal features.

questions.stem: An organism with no membrane-bounded organelles in its cell, belongs to the kingdom
questions.explanation: Monera (bacteria, blue-green algae) are prokaryotes without a nuclear membrane or membrane-bound organelles.

questions.topic: Complexity of organization in higher organisms
questions.stem: Which of the following attributes can be regarded as an advantage of complexity in higher organisms?
options: Cellular differentiation leads to loss of independence of cells
Cellular differentiation leads to internal structural specialization
Cellular differentiation occurs in only few cells
questions.explanation: Differentiation produces specialised tissues and organs that do particular jobs efficiently; loss of cell independence is a disadvantage.

questions.topic: Forms in which Living Cells Exist
questions.stem: One characteristic feature of Chlamydomonas is
options: the presence of nucleus in its cell.
questions.explanation: Chlamydomonas has a single cup-shaped chloroplast with a pyrenoid.

questions.stem: Movement in Euglena is brought about by
questions.explanation: Euglena swims by the lashing (whip-like) movement of its flagellum.

questions.stem: The major difference between osmosis and diffusion is that in osmosis
options: cells take up nutrients and water.
oxygen and water move from one part of the organism to another.
carbon dioxide and water are eliminated from the organism.
water moves through the cell membrane.
questions.explanation: Osmosis is the movement of water molecules across a semi-permeable membrane.

questions.stem: The smell of perfume perceived from a distance is made possible by the process of
questions.explanation: Perfume molecules spread from high to low concentration through the air by diffusion.

questions.stem: Aerobic respiration in the cell takes place in the
questions.explanation: The Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation of aerobic respiration occur in mitochondria.

questions.topic: Irritability as a Basic Characteristic of Protoplasm
questions.stem: The mimosa plant shows nastic movement whenever it is touched, this is due to changes in
options: transpiration pull on the petal base.
tugor pressure at the leaf base.
questions.explanation: Touch causes cells of the pulvinus at the leaf base to lose turgor, so the leaflets fold.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not true of asexual reproduction in a living organism? It
options: results in the formation of two daughter cells.
involves only division of somatic cells.
involves mitotic division of a cell.
questions.explanation: Fusion of gametes is sexual reproduction; asexual reproduction involves mitosis only.

questions.stem: In which of the following vessels will a drug injected into the upper arm enters the heart?
questions.explanation: Blood from the arms returns via the subclavian veins to the superior (anterior) vena cava and the right atrium.

questions.stem: The 'Lub' sound of the heartbeat is due to the flapping close of the
questions.explanation: 'Lub' is produced when the atrioventricular (tricuspid and bicuspid) valves close at the start of ventricular systole; 'dub' is the semilunar valves.

questions.stem: A flower has its stigma above the anther and the anther always ripens before the stigma. What type of pollination will be possible in this type of floral arrangement?
questions.explanation: Protandry (anthers ripening first) and a stigma placed above the anthers prevent self-pollination, so cross-pollination occurs.

questions.stem: A monoecious plant bears
options: perfect staminate flowers on the same plant.
staminate and pistillate flowers on the same plant.
perfect and pistillate flowers on different plants.
pistillate and staminate flowers on different plants.
questions.explanation: Monoecious plants (e.g. maize) carry separate male and female flowers on the same plant.

questions.stem: Which of the following insects is not an agent of pollination?
questions.explanation: Bees, butterflies and moths visit flowers for nectar; termites feed on wood and do not pollinate.

questions.stem: A plant with one seed leaf in its seed and the floral parts of its flowers in groups of three will likely be
questions.explanation: Monocots have one cotyledon and flower parts in threes.

questions.topic: Movement of water to the apex of trees and herbs
questions.stem: A boy puts a straw inside a bottle of coke and observed that the liquid moved up the straw to a level higher than that of the liquid in the bottle. What is the importance of the observed process to the movement of water in plants? It helps plants to
options: move water up the xylem vessels.
move water from the root hairs to the cortex.
questions.explanation: The rise of liquid in a narrow tube is capillarity, which contributes to the rise of water in narrow xylem vessels.

questions.stem: Energy is required for each of the following activities except
questions.explanation: Gaseous exchange takes place by passive diffusion and needs no energy from the cell, unlike active transport and muscle contraction.

questions.stem: The elements necessary for the formation of chlorophyll in the leaf of a plant are
questions.explanation: Magnesium and nitrogen are parts of the chlorophyll molecule and iron is needed for its synthesis.

questions.stem: A patient's blood was unable to clot on time so the doctor advised him to take more of vitamin
questions.explanation: Vitamin K is needed to make prothrombin and other clotting factors.

questions.stem: A person suffering from exophthalmic goitre would have all of the following symptoms except
questions.explanation: Bleeding gums is a sign of scurvy (vitamin C deficiency), not a thyroid disorder.

questions.stem: The ultimate source of energy is
questions.explanation: All energy in food chains and fossil fuels comes originally from sunlight trapped by photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Organisms that occupy the second trophic level are called
questions.explanation: Primary consumers (herbivores) feed on producers at the first trophic level.

questions.stem: The feature that prevents water loss from the body of a lizard is the
questions.explanation: The dry, horny epidermal scales of reptiles reduce water loss.

questions.stem: Which of the following characteristics is not found in arid land animals?
questions.explanation: A broad flat body has a large surface area that would increase water loss; desert animals show the other features.

questions.stem: The following conditions are associated with smoking of cigarettes except
questions.explanation: Smoking is linked to heart disease, low birth weight and impaired reflexes; arthritis is not a recognised effect.

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms may bring about reduction in human population?
questions.explanation: Houseflies carry germs of cholera, typhoid and dysentery, which can kill many people.

questions.stem: Population is defined as
options: the number of individual organisms per unit area.
a progressive series of changes over a period of time in a human community.
the total number of organisms of the same species living together in a given period of time.
the total number of different species of communities living in an environment in a given period of time.
questions.explanation: A population is the total number of organisms of one species living in a particular place at a given time.

questions.stem: The following statements are true about climax communities except that
options: the community is at its equilibrium.
species of plants and animals can change from year to year.
the vegetation reaches the highest development.
questions.explanation: A climax community is stable with little change in species composition.

questions.stem: Poisonous substances produced by bacteria in plants or animal bodies are called
questions.explanation: Bacterial poisons are toxins.

questions.stem: Which of the following natural resources is non-renewable?
questions.explanation: Solid minerals form over geological time and cannot be replaced once used.

questions.stem: Which of the following occurrences is not an advantage of forest conservation?
questions.explanation: Timber production involves felling trees; the others are conservation benefits.

questions.stem: Importance of conservation of wildlife include the following except
options: generation of income through sale of ivory.
maintaining the balance of the ecosystem.
questions.explanation: Ivory sales encourage poaching of elephants, which is contrary to conservation.

questions.stem: A mother is likely to be able to distinguish between her identical twin daughters because of
questions.explanation: Identical twins are genetically alike; the mother uses small visible (morphological) differences.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors does not contribute to variations in living organisms?
questions.explanation: Mitosis produces genetically identical cells; meiosis, mutation and environment cause variation.

questions.stem: Which of the following traits shows clear-cut differences with no intermediate forms?
questions.explanation: Sex is discontinuous (male or female); intelligence and skin colour are continuous.

questions.stem: Variation in organisms can be described as when the
options: organisms feed on different types of food.
organisms show different traits from each other.
organisms are living in different communities.
questions.explanation: Variation is the differences in characteristics among individuals of a species.

questions.stem: The simplest unit for transfer of character from parents to offspring is the
questions.explanation: The gene is the basic unit of heredity.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about chromosomes is correct?
options: In kidney cells of diploid organisms, chromosomes occur singly
In gametes, chromosomes occur in pairs
A given species always has a varying number of homologous chromosomes
In gonads, chromosomes occur in pairs
questions.explanation: Gonad (body) cells are diploid with homologous pairs; only the gametes are haploid.

questions.stem: Deoxyribonucleic acid is most suitable for the transmission of information from generation to generation through chromosomes because it
options: is made up of anti-parallel chains.
is made up of a sugar, an acid and a base.
questions.explanation: DNA can copy itself exactly, so genetic information is passed on to daughter cells and offspring.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct about genes? They
options: are usually affected by the environment.
questions.explanation: An individual's genes remain the same throughout life (barring mutation).

questions.stem: The major difference between genotype and phenotype is that phenotype
options: is an observable trait while genotype is a dominant character.
is an observable trait while genotype is a recessive character.
is the sum total of observable traits while genotype is the sum total of dominant and recessive genes.
is an observed feature in female offspring while genotype is the sum total of genes inherited in male offspring.
questions.explanation: Phenotype is the observable characteristics; genotype is the genetic make-up (both dominant and recessive alleles).

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true about carriers of sickle cell trait?
options: They are often short of blood
All their blood cells are sickle-shaped
questions.explanation: AS carriers are usually healthy and are relatively resistant to malaria.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman was successfully transfused with blood from her husband who has blood group AB. What is the blood group of the woman?
questions.explanation: Group AB blood carries A and B antigens, so it can only be given to an AB recipient (universal recipient).

questions.stem: The caste that carries out tail-waggling dance in bees is the
questions.explanation: Worker bees perform the waggle dance to show other workers the direction and distance of food.

questions.stem: The process of natural selection results in
questions.explanation: Insecticide resistance arises naturally as resistant mosquitoes survive and breed; the others result from artificial selection or breeding.

questions.stem: Larmack's theory of evolution consists of the following except
options: use and disuse of body parts.
questions.explanation: Survival of the fittest belongs to Darwin's theory of natural selection.

questions.stem: The major reason why Mendel covered artificially pollinated flowers with small paper bag was to
options: prevent pollen grains from being carried away by insects.
prevent pollen grains from being carried away by rainwater.
prevent the chance of natural pollution.
questions.explanation: Bagging prevented unwanted natural pollination ('pollution' in the print) by foreign pollen.

questions.stem: A student defined chromosome as a thread-like material found in the cytoplasm. What is wrong with the definition? Its
questions.explanation: Chromosomes are found in the nucleus, not the cytoplasm.

questions.stem:
(a)(i) What is primary growth in flowering plants? [2 marks]
(ii) State four ways in which primary growth is of importance to plants. [4 marks]
(b) Describe growth in a named insect. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Primary growth is the increase in length of stem and root due to cell division at the apical meristems (shoot and root tips)
1 mark: (a)(ii) Increases height so the plant gets more light
1 mark: (a)(ii) Roots grow deeper to absorb more water and mineral salts and anchor the plant
1 mark: (a)(ii) Produces new leaves, branches and flowers
1 mark: (a)(ii) Forms the primary tissues (epidermis, cortex, vascular bundles)
1 mark: (b) Named insect, e.g. cockroach (incomplete metamorphosis) or housefly/butterfly
2 marks: (b) The insect has a hard chitinous exoskeleton that cannot stretch, so growth is discontinuous/occurs in stages
2 marks: (b) The young (nymph) grows until the cuticle is tight; it then moults (ecdysis), shedding the old cuticle under hormonal control
2 marks: (b) The body swells by taking in air/water and the new soft cuticle hardens; the period between moults is an instar
1 mark: (b) The cockroach nymph moults about 6-7 times, gaining wings and reproductive organs at the final moult to become an adult
questions.explanation: (a)(i) Primary growth is the increase in length of a flowering plant's stem and root caused by cell division at the apical meristems of the shoot and root tips, followed by cell elongation and differentiation. (ii) It raises the shoot to get more light for photosynthesis, extends the roots deeper for water, minerals and anchorage, produces new leaves, branches and flowers, and forms the primary tissues such as epidermis, cortex and vascular bundles. (b) In the cockroach the body is covered by a rigid chitinous exoskeleton that cannot expand, so growth takes place in steps. The egg hatches into a nymph resembling the adult but without wings. The nymph feeds and grows until the cuticle becomes tight; it then moults (ecdysis), controlled by the hormone ecdysone: the old cuticle splits and is shed, the insect swells by swallowing air, and the new soft cuticle hardens. Each stage between moults is an instar. After about six or seven moults the nymph acquires wings and mature reproductive organs and becomes an adult, which no longer moults. Growth is therefore step-like rather than continuous.

questions.topic: Skeleton and supporting systems in animals
questions.stem:
(a)(i) Name two types of moveable joints in mammals. [2 marks]
(ii) Name the features of the moveable joint and how they serve to protect the joint. [6 marks]
(b)(i) Define translocation in plants. [3 marks]
(ii) Describe the ringing experiment to demonstrate translocation in plants. [9 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a)(i) Ball and socket joint (e.g. shoulder, hip)
1 mark: (a)(i) Hinge joint (e.g. elbow, knee); also pivot or gliding joints
2 marks: (a)(ii) Articular cartilage covers the ends of the bones, reducing friction and absorbing shock
2 marks: (a)(ii) Synovial membrane secretes synovial fluid, which lubricates the joint and nourishes the cartilage
2 marks: (a)(ii) Ligaments hold the bones together and prevent dislocation; the capsule encloses the joint
3 marks: (b)(i) Translocation is the movement of manufactured food (sugars, amino acids) in solution from the leaves to other parts of the plant through the phloem
2 marks: (b)(ii) Select a woody (e.g. hibiscus) stem; remove a complete ring of bark (including phloem) without damaging the xylem
1 mark: (b)(ii) Leave a similar unringed stem as control
2 marks: (b)(ii) After some weeks the bark just above the ring swells while the part below shrinks
2 marks: (b)(ii) Tests show food (sugar/starch) accumulates above the ring; leaves above do not wilt since xylem still carries water
2 marks: (b)(ii) Conclusion: manufactured food moves downwards through the phloem (in the bark) and not the xylem
questions.explanation: (a)(i) Movable (synovial) joints include the ball and socket joint at the shoulder and hip and the hinge joint at the elbow and knee. (ii) The ends of the bones are covered by smooth articular cartilage, which reduces friction and absorbs shock. The synovial membrane lining the joint capsule secretes synovial fluid, which lubricates the joint and nourishes the cartilage. Tough ligaments bind the bones together and, with the capsule, prevent dislocation. (b)(i) Translocation is the transport of manufactured food such as sugars and amino acids in solution from the leaves (sources) to growing points and storage organs through the phloem. (ii) Choose a woody shoot and carefully remove a complete ring of bark, which contains the phloem, leaving the xylem intact; keep an unringed shoot as control. After some weeks the region just above the ring swells, while the region below shrinks; food tests show sugar and starch accumulating above the ring. The leaves stay turgid because the xylem still conducts water. This shows that food is translocated through the phloem.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain the following terms:
(i) test cross;
(ii) recessive allele;
(iii) homozygote. [8 marks]
(b)(i) Why is sickle-cell anaemia considered a deadly disease? [5 marks]
(ii) Explain briefly how sickle-cell anaemia can be reduced in a population. [6 marks]
(iii) State one advantage which a carrier of the sickle-cell anaemia trait has. [1 mark]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) Test cross: crossing an organism showing the dominant trait (unknown genotype) with a homozygous recessive to find out whether it is homozygous or heterozygous
2 marks: (a)(ii) Recessive allele: an allele whose effect is masked by the dominant allele and is expressed only in the homozygous condition
3 marks: (a)(iii) Homozygote: an organism having two identical alleles of a gene (e.g. TT or tt); it breeds true
2 marks: (b)(i) The red cells become sickle-shaped and rigid, carry less oxygen and are destroyed quickly, causing severe anaemia
2 marks: (b)(i) Sickle cells block capillaries, causing painful crises and damage to organs (e.g. spleen, kidney, brain/stroke)
1 mark: (b)(i) Sufferers have low resistance to infections and often die young; there is no simple cure
2 marks: (b)(ii) Genotype testing of intending couples before marriage
2 marks: (b)(ii) Genetic counselling: carriers (AS) are advised not to marry other carriers (AS or SS)
2 marks: (b)(ii) Public enlightenment/education on the inheritance of the disease
1 mark: (b)(iii) The carrier (AS) has greater resistance to malaria
questions.explanation: (a)(i) A test cross is a cross between an organism showing a dominant trait but of unknown genotype and a homozygous recessive individual; if all offspring show the dominant trait the organism is homozygous, but a 1:1 ratio shows it is heterozygous. (ii) A recessive allele is one whose effect is hidden in the presence of the dominant allele and appears only when two copies are present. (iii) A homozygote has two identical alleles of a gene, e.g. TT or tt, and breeds true. (b)(i) In SS individuals the haemoglobin is abnormal, so red cells become sickle-shaped and rigid; they carry less oxygen and are rapidly destroyed, causing severe anaemia. The cells block small vessels, causing painful crises and damage to organs such as the spleen, kidneys and brain, lowering resistance to infection and often causing early death. (ii) It can be reduced by genotype testing before marriage, genetic counselling so that carriers do not marry other carriers, and public education about its inheritance. (iii) A carrier (AS) is more resistant to malaria.

questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Pollution is the introduction of harmful substances or energy (pollutants) into the environment by man in amounts that harm living things
2 marks: (a)(ii) Overcrowding is a situation where the population of organisms is greater than the available space and resources (food, water, shelter) can support
3 marks: (b)(i) Water pollutants: sewage, crude oil, industrial effluents/chemicals, fertilisers, pesticides, refuse (any three)
3 marks: (b)(ii) Air pollutants: carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, smoke/soot, dust, nitrogen oxides, lead compounds (any three)
5 marks: (c)(i) Treat sewage before discharge; treat industrial wastes; prevent oil spills; avoid dumping refuse in water; control use of fertilisers and pesticides; enforce anti-pollution laws (any five)
5 marks: (c)(ii) Fit filters/scrubbers to factory chimneys; maintain vehicles/use unleaded fuel; avoid bush burning and burning of refuse; site industries away from residential areas; reduce gas flaring; plant trees; enforce laws (any five)
questions.explanation: (a)(i) Pollution is the release by human activity of substances or energy into air, water or land in amounts that are harmful to living things or the environment. (ii) Overcrowding is when the number of organisms in an area exceeds the available space, food and other resources, leading to competition, disease and poor health. (b)(i) Water pollutants include sewage, crude oil and industrial effluents (also fertilisers and pesticides). (ii) Air pollutants include carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide and smoke (also dust and nitrogen oxides). (c)(i) Water pollution can be prevented by treating sewage and industrial wastes before discharge, preventing oil spillage, not dumping refuse into water bodies, controlling the use of fertilisers and pesticides, and enforcing environmental laws. (ii) Air pollution can be prevented by fitting filters to factory chimneys, servicing vehicles and using clean fuels, stopping bush burning and open burning of refuse, reducing gas flaring, locating factories away from homes, planting trees and enforcing regulations.

questions.stem:
(a)(i) State three reasons why organisms are classified. [3 marks]
(b)(i) Name three kingdoms into which living organisms are classified. [3 marks]
(ii) Give one example each of organisms belonging to the kingdoms named in 5(b)(i) above. [3 marks]
(c)(i) Describe the structure of a named fungus. [8 marks]
(ii) Outline three activities of fungi which are beneficial to man. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) To make the study of the large number of organisms easier
1 mark: (a) To show relationships between organisms (and evolution)
1 mark: (a) For easy identification and naming of organisms
3 marks: (b)(i) Any three: Monera, Protista (Protoctista), Fungi, Plantae, Animalia
3 marks: (b)(ii) Examples: Monera - bacteria; Protista - Amoeba/Paramecium; Fungi - Rhizopus/mushroom; Plantae - fern/maize; Animalia - toad/man
1 mark: (c)(i) Named fungus, e.g. Rhizopus (bread mould)
2 marks: (c)(i) The body (mycelium) consists of a network of fine, branched, white threads called hyphae, which are coenocytic (non-septate) with many nuclei
2 marks: (c)(i) Stolons run over the surface and rhizoids penetrate the food substrate, secreting enzymes and absorbing nutrients
2 marks: (c)(i) Erect sporangiophores arise from the stolons, each bearing a black spherical sporangium containing many spores, with a columella inside
1 mark: (c)(i) The wall is made of chitin; there is no chlorophyll, so it feeds saprophytically
1 mark: (c)(ii) Yeast is used in brewing and baking (fermentation)
1 mark: (c)(ii) Production of antibiotics, e.g. penicillin from Penicillium
1 mark: (c)(ii) Decomposition of dead matter to recycle nutrients; mushrooms are eaten as food
questions.explanation: (a) Organisms are classified to make the study of the vast number of living things easier, to show their relationships and evolutionary history, and to aid identification and naming. (b)(i) Living things are placed in kingdoms such as Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. (ii) Examples: Monera - bacteria; Fungi - Rhizopus; Animalia - toad. (c)(i) Rhizopus (bread mould) has a mycelium made of white, branched, thread-like hyphae that are non-septate and multinucleate, with chitin walls and no chlorophyll. Horizontal hyphae (stolons) spread over the food, and at intervals rhizoids grow into it, secreting digestive enzymes and absorbing the products (saprophytic nutrition). Erect sporangiophores arise above the rhizoids, each ending in a round black sporangium with a central columella and many spores, which are released when the wall bursts. (ii) Fungi benefit man: yeasts ferment sugar in brewing and bread-making, Penicillium yields penicillin, and fungi decompose dead matter, recycling nutrients; mushrooms are also food.

questions.stem:
(a)(i) Name three organisms found in the soil. [3 marks]
(ii) State two ways by which each of the organisms named in 6(a)(i) above maintain soil fertility. [6 marks]
(b)(i) Outline the role of DNA in protein synthesis. [6 marks]
(ii) If a cell actively synthesizes proteins, name three organelles that are likely to be abundant in the cell. [3 marks]
(c) What is first aid? [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) Earthworm, bacteria, fungi (also termites, millipedes)
2 marks: (a)(ii) Earthworm: burrows aerate and drain the soil; its casts mix the soil and add organic matter
2 marks: (a)(ii) Bacteria: decompose dead matter to release nutrients; fix atmospheric nitrogen (Rhizobium, Azotobacter); nitrification
2 marks: (a)(ii) Fungi: decompose organic matter to form humus; form mycorrhizae that help plants absorb nutrients
2 marks: (b)(i) DNA in the nucleus carries the genetic code for the sequence of amino acids in proteins
2 marks: (b)(i) The code is transcribed into messenger RNA, which moves out of the nucleus to the ribosomes
2 marks: (b)(i) At the ribosomes transfer RNA brings amino acids, which are joined in the order dictated by the mRNA code to form the protein
3 marks: (b)(ii) Ribosomes, rough endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi bodies (also mitochondria, nucleolus)
2 marks: (c) First aid is the immediate, temporary help given to an injured or sick person before qualified medical help is obtained
questions.explanation: (a)(i) Soil organisms include earthworms, bacteria and fungi. (ii) Earthworms burrow, aerating and draining the soil, and their casts mix the soil layers and add organic matter. Bacteria decompose dead organisms, releasing mineral nutrients, and nitrogen-fixing and nitrifying bacteria increase soil nitrates. Fungi break down organic matter into humus and form mycorrhizal associations that help roots absorb nutrients. (b)(i) DNA in the nucleus carries the genetic code: the sequence of its bases specifies the sequence of amino acids in a protein. The code is copied (transcribed) into messenger RNA, which passes out to the ribosomes in the cytoplasm. There, transfer RNA molecules bring specific amino acids, which are linked in the order specified by the mRNA codons (translation) to form the polypeptide. (ii) Such a cell will have many ribosomes, much rough endoplasmic reticulum and well-developed Golgi bodies (plus many mitochondria for energy). (c) First aid is the immediate, temporary care given to an injured or suddenly ill person before professional medical help arrives.

questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) Parasitism: an association in which one organism (parasite) lives in or on another (host), obtaining food from it and harming it
1 mark: (a)(i) Example: tapeworm in man, louse/tick on cattle, mistletoe/dodder on plants
3 marks: (a)(ii) Saprophytism: a mode of nutrition in which an organism feeds on dead and decaying organic matter, digesting it externally and absorbing the products
1 mark: (a)(ii) Example: Rhizopus, mushroom, bacteria of decay
3 marks: (a)(iii) Symbiosis (mutualism): a close association between two organisms of different species in which both benefit
1 mark: (a)(iii) Example: Rhizobium in root nodules of legumes; lichen (alga and fungus); cellulose-digesting bacteria in ruminants
1 mark: (b) Named ectoparasite, e.g. tick (or louse, flea)
2 marks: (b) Body flattened dorso-ventrally, allowing it to lie close to the host's skin and avoid being dislodged
2 marks: (b) Legs with claws/hooks for clinging firmly to the host's hair or skin
2 marks: (b) Piercing and sucking mouthparts (hypostome with backward teeth) for piercing the skin, sucking blood and anchoring
1 mark: (b) Hard, tough cuticle/expandable body to resist scratching and store large blood meals; brown colour for camouflage
questions.explanation: (a)(i) Parasitism is an association in which one organism, the parasite, lives on or in another, the host, deriving food and shelter from it and harming it, e.g. the tapeworm in man or the tick on cattle. (ii) Saprophytism is nutrition on dead or decaying organic matter, which is digested externally by secreted enzymes and the products absorbed, e.g. Rhizopus and mushrooms. (iii) Symbiosis (mutualism) is a close association between organisms of two different species in which both benefit, e.g. Rhizobium bacteria in legume root nodules, which fix nitrogen for the plant and receive food and shelter. (b) The cattle tick has an oval, dorso-ventrally flattened body that lies close to the host's skin and is not easily brushed off. Its four pairs of legs bear claws for gripping the hair and skin. Its mouthparts include a hypostome with backward-pointing teeth for piercing the skin, sucking blood and anchoring firmly. Its tough, leathery and highly expandable body resists scratching and can hold a large blood meal, so it feeds infrequently, and its brownish colour camouflages it.

questions.stem:
(a) State three ways by which water is of importance to mammals. [3 marks]
(b) Name:
(i) two structures in plants;
(ii) three structures in mammals; that excrete water. [5 marks]
(c) How does the mammalian body respond to low water content? [8 marks]
(d) List four plant hormones. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) Solvent/medium for chemical reactions in cells
1 mark: (a) Transport medium (blood plasma, lymph) and for excretion of wastes in urine
1 mark: (a) Temperature regulation through sweating; lubrication of joints; digestion (hydrolysis)
2 marks: (b)(i) Stomata and lenticels (also hydathodes)
3 marks: (b)(ii) Kidneys, skin (sweat glands), lungs
2 marks: (c) Low water content raises the osmotic pressure (concentration) of the blood, detected by osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus
2 marks: (c) The pituitary gland releases more antidiuretic hormone (ADH) into the blood
2 marks: (c) ADH makes the distal convoluted tubules and collecting ducts more permeable, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced
2 marks: (c) The person feels thirsty and drinks; sweating is also reduced, restoring normal water content
4 marks: (d) Auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid, ethylene (any four)
questions.explanation: (a) Water is the solvent in which cell reactions take place, the medium of transport in blood and lymph and for removal of wastes in urine, and it helps regulate body temperature through sweating, as well as lubricating joints and taking part in digestion. (b)(i) Plants lose water through stomata and lenticels. (ii) In mammals water is excreted by the kidneys, the skin (sweat glands) and the lungs. (c) When body water is low, the blood becomes more concentrated; osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect this and stimulate the posterior pituitary to secrete more antidiuretic hormone. ADH increases the permeability of the distal tubules and collecting ducts, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood and only a small amount of concentrated urine is passed. At the same time the thirst centre makes the person drink, and sweating is reduced, until the water balance is restored (negative feedback). (d) Plant hormones include auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins and abscisic acid (also ethylene).
